ambiguity.note: The ampersand construction can mean John Smith and Mary Smith, or John (no surname) and Mary Smith; segmentation is undecided.

text: Invitations were sent to John & Mary Smith last week.
title: Two given names joined by an ampersand before a shared surname
why: 'John & Mary Smith' leaves 'Smith' attached only to the second name in a strict reading; the span convention treats the sequence as ambiguous in segmentation.

text: As shown by Nguyen et al., the effect persists.
title: Surname followed by 'et al.'
why: 'et al.' is a Latin abbreviation, not part of the name, and its period is part of the abbreviation.

title: Two names on consecutive lines in a signature block
why: A newline is the only separator between two names; sentence- or line-based preprocessing must not merge them into one span.

title: Two names in a pipe-separated table row
why: A text table row where the pipe character is the only delimiter.

ambiguity.note: Nothing indicates whether this is one three-token name or several adjacent names.

text: Please contact Sam Lee Kim for tickets.
title: Three adjacent tokens that may be one, two or three people
why: 'Sam Lee Kim' can be a single person with a middle name, 'Sam Lee' plus 'Kim', or three people. The text does not decide; the case is recorded as honest ambiguity of segmentation.

ambiguity.note: Adjacent two-token names could be re-segmented (for example a double surname), but three repeated given-plus-surname pairs make the intended three-person reading the natural one.

text: Present were Maria Lopez Ahmed Hassan Chen Wei at the table.
title: Three full names written one after another without separators
why: Attendee lists sometimes run names together separated only by spaces. The boundaries between names must be inferred, not read from punctuation.

text: Dr. Nakamura, Prof. Aaltonen, and Mr. Pierce signed the letter.
title: Several titled surnames in a list
why: Each title is excluded and each surname is its own span, with commas and 'and' between them.

title: Two surnames joined by 'and' in a citation
why: In scholarly text, authors are cited by surname alone; the year after is not part of either span.

title: Full name inside an ALL-CAPS headline
why: ALL CAPS removes the initial-capital cue for every word, so names are indistinguishable from other words by case.

text: ok so maria lopez signed it yesterday
title: Full name written entirely in lowercase
why: Informal messages drop capitalization, removing the cue most simple name detectors depend on.

title: Lowercase given name as an addressee
why: A lowercase vocative in chat text, where the only cues are the greeting word and the comma.

ambiguity.note: The first 'may' opens a polite question (modal); the second follows the verb 'ask' as its addressee.

text: may i ask may about it
title: Lowercase 'may' as both modal and name candidate
why: In lowercase chat, 'may' as a modal and 'may' as a person cannot be told apart by case; only syntax separates them.

text: ask dr nakamura about the scans
title: Lowercase surname after a title in casual text
why: A lowercase surname after 'dr' in chat text; the lowercase title is excluded like its capitalized form.

title: Name with an internal capital in the middle of a word
why: A name with unusual internal capitalization (DeShawn). Tokenizers that lowercase or split at capitals alter the name.

ambiguity.note: Here the given name precedes a surname-like token, which together name a person; 'Baker' is the occupation before the name.

text: Local Baker Olivia Brandt Wins National Award
title: Title Case headline that names a person
why: Partner of the Baker headline: a given name plus surname in Title Case among other capitalized words.

ambiguity.note: The adjective 'Local' before it marks the occupation noun; no given name accompanies it.

title: Title Case headline where an occupation noun looks like a surname
why: In headline Title Case every content word is capitalized, so Baker (occupation) looks like a surname. There is no person in this headline.

text: John Smith signed the contract on Tuesday.
title: Common two-token name in a plain sentence
why: Control case: a very common given name plus surname in an unremarkable sentence. Easy positives are authored explicitly so that slice counts show how much of the corpus is easy.

text: Please ask Emily to join the call.
title: Common given name alone mid-sentence
why: Control case: a single-token given name with no surname or title, so any detector relying on multi-token structure has nothing else to lean on.

text: The courier handed Michael the signed forms.
title: Common given name as the indirect object
why: Control case: a PERSON in a ditransitive sentence, at a position where common words usually appear.

text: Nobody had heard from Robert Taylor since the merger.
title: Common full name as the object of a preposition
why: Control case: a PERSON in a prepositional phrase far from the sentence start, where capitalization is the only cue.

text: The award went to Jessica Wilson.
title: Common full name immediately before the sentence period
why: Control case: the sentence-final period is not part of the name, so the expected span stops before it.

text: The report was reviewed by Johnson before publication.
title: Common surname alone as the agent of a verb
why: Control case: a surname used alone, as newspapers and reports do, with a clear human-agent role ('reviewed by').

text: Sarah Miller and David Brown met the client.
title: Two common full names in one sentence
why: Control case with two PERSON mentions, to check that every mention is expected rather than only the first.

title: Two short common given names joined by 'and'
why: Control case: very short single-token names (three letters) that tokenizers may merge with neighbours or ignore.

ambiguity.note: A surname-like second token and the phone-call predicate select a person.

text: April Reyes called the supplier this morning.
title: April as a person who made a call
why: Partner of april-showers-month: April as a given name with a human-action predicate.

ambiguity.note: The idiom 'April showers' is a fixed phrase about weather in the month.

title: April in an idiom about weather
why: April is a month and a given name; in the idiom 'April showers' it is the month.

ambiguity.note: The lowercase word modifies the noun 'hall' and means dignified.

title: Lowercase august as an adjective
why: 'August' is a month, a given name, and (lowercase) an adjective meaning dignified.

ambiguity.note: The determiner 'the' and lowercase spelling make the second occurrence a noun.

text: Bill paid the bill on Friday.
title: Person and invoice spelled Bill
why: A person and an invoice with the same spelling: the first is the subject of 'paid', the second the object after a determiner.

ambiguity.note: Both a person and a bank can contact someone, and the sentence adds no further cue.

title: Chase as a bank or a person
why: Chase is a bank name and a given name; 'contacted us this morning' fits both a person and an institution.

ambiguity.note: The first word is the subject of 'arrived by taxi', which only a person can do; after 'before' the lowercase word is the time of day.

text: Dawn arrived by taxi before dawn.
title: Sentence-initial name 'Dawn' and lowercase noun 'dawn'
why: Two occurrences of the same letters in one sentence with opposite expectations: person first, time-of-day noun second.

ambiguity.note: Sending a draft to X takes human recipients.

text: Send the draft to Faith and Hope tonight.
title: Virtue-noun names as recipients
why: Two virtue nouns that are also names, used as recipients of a message.

ambiguity.note: After 'had to', the bare lowercase word is a verb meaning to wade across.

text: We had to ford the stream on foot.
title: Lowercase 'ford' as a verb
why: Lowercase decoy: to ford a stream. Included so brand/surname detectors do not fire on the bare letters.

ambiguity.note: Title plus a signing action selects the surname over the brand.

title: Ford as a surname after Mrs.
why: Ford is a car brand, a river crossing and a surname; with a title and signing action it is a person.

ambiguity.note: 'forward to' takes recipients and the bare capitalized words are in the recipient position.

text: Please forward this to Hunter and Mason.
title: Two occupation-word names as recipients
why: 'forward this to X and Y' needs two recipients; both capitalized words are occupation nouns that are also names.

ambiguity.note: A state or country can be said to win an election, as can a person named Georgia.

title: Georgia in a sentence about winning
why: Georgia is a state, a country and a given name; 'won the election' fits a place (as metonym for its voters) and a person.

ambiguity.note: The only verb is 'Resume'; 'Frank Talks' is its subject noun phrase with an adjective modifier.

title: Title Case headline starting with an adjective that is a name
why: In Title Case every word is capitalized, so 'Frank' carries no name evidence; 'Frank Talks Resume After Delay' is a noun phrase and a verb phrase about negotiations.

ambiguity.note: A plant can be everywhere on a hillside and a person can be everywhere socially.

title: Heather as a plant or a person
why: Heather is a plant and a given name; 'was everywhere that summer' fits both.

ambiguity.note: A comma-set non-restrictive clause attaches to a definite referent; a bare singular count noun without a determiner is not grammatical as a common noun here, so the word is a name.

text: Hunter, who tracked the deer all night, finally rested.
title: Hunter with an appositive relative clause
why: A name that is also an occupation noun, followed by a comma and a relative clause, which is the standard shape of a named referent.

ambiguity.note: The plural ending and the restrictive relative clause without a comma mark a generic noun phrase.

text: Hunters who tracked the deer all night finally rested.
title: Hunters as a plural occupation noun
why: Partner of hunter-appositive-clause: the plural -s makes a generic noun, so the capitalized first word is not a person.

ambiguity.note: A climbing plant and a person can both be by a wall.

text: Ivy was by the north wall.
title: Ivy as a plant or a person
why: Ivy is a plant and a given name; being by the north wall fits both.

ambiguity.note: Thanking and giving a lift are human actions.

text: Jack thanked Sage for the lift.
title: Two tool or herb words as the subject and object of thanking
why: 'thanked' requires an animate subject and object, so both capitalized words are names even though each is also an ordinary noun.

ambiguity.note: A tool can be missing from a toolbox; a person could be missing from a group figuratively called the toolbox. The text does not exclude either, though the tool reading is likelier.

text: Jack was missing from the toolbox.
title: Jack as a tool or a person
why: Jack is a tool and a very common given name; 'missing from the toolbox' fits both.

ambiguity.note: 'Jordan' followed by a surname-like token and an agentive verb is a person, not the country.

title: Jordan as the given name in a full name
why: A full name whose first token is also a country. The span covers both tokens.

ambiguity.note: Only a person can be asked to bring a laptop.

text: Please ask Jordan to bring the laptop.
title: Jordan as a given name used alone
why: Jordan is a country, a river and a very common given name. Here a request to bring a laptop selects a person.

ambiguity.note: A report can mention a country, a river or a person equally well.

text: Jordan was mentioned twice in the report.
title: Jordan mentioned in a report with no other cue
why: 'Jordan' is a country, a river and a person; 'was mentioned twice in the report' fits any of them. Recorded as honest ambiguity.

ambiguity.note: 'With her sister' needs a person as the first subject; after 'in' the second word is a month.

text: June arrives in June with her sister.
title: June as a person arriving in the month of June
why: A name and a month with the same spelling in one sentence.

ambiguity.note: 'ask X to send the file' takes a person as X.

text: can you ask hunter to send the file
title: Common-word name in lowercase chat
why: In lowercase chat 'hunter' is a name only if the verb frame asks for a person.

ambiguity.note: No comma follows 'Mark' and the next words form a verb phrase with an object, so it is an imperative.

text: Mark the boxes before they ship.
title: Mark as an imperative verb
why: 'Mark the boxes before they ship' is an instruction. A sentence-initial capitalized imperative verb has the shape of a name.

ambiguity.note: A comma separates the address term from a full clause.

title: Mark as a vocative
why: Partner of mark-imperative-verb: the comma after the word and a following independent clause make it a vocative.

ambiguity.note: Both words are given names, but the 'from ... through' date-range frame requires months.

text: The audit runs from May through June.
title: May and June both used as months
why: Both words are also given names. In a date range they are months; a detector keyed on surface form alone will tag both.

ambiguity.note: The first 'May' follows the preposition 'in' (a month); the second is the subject of 'will attend' (a person).

text: The meeting is in May and May will attend.
title: Same surface form 'May' as a month and as a person in one sentence
why: The canonical example from the project docs: context, not the word, determines whether PERSON is emitted. Both readings appear in one sentence so a single global decision cannot be right.

ambiguity.note: 'Ask X whether' requires a person as the addressee.

text: Ask May whether the review is ready.
title: May as a person being asked a question
why: The imperative 'Ask May whether ...' needs an animate addressee. Tests whether a month-biased detector over-suppresses real names.

ambiguity.note: 'May 5th' is a date; a person name is not followed by an ordinal day number.

title: May followed by a day number
why: A month-day expression: the number after 'May' is the strongest cue that this is a date.

ambiguity.note: The first token is capitalized and followed by a surname; 'for miles' is a distance expression.

title: Given name 'Miles' next to the common noun 'miles'
why: The unit word 'miles' (lowercase) follows a full name 'Miles Carter'; checks that the name and the noun are not merged.

ambiguity.note: 'The baker' is a common noun with a definite article; 'Marcus Baker' is a full name.

text: The baker delivered bread to Marcus Baker on Monday.
title: Occupation noun 'baker' beside the surname 'Baker'
why: Occupational surnames are also ordinary nouns. The lowercase occupation is not a person mention here; the capitalized surname after a given name is.

ambiguity.note: Title plus an approving agent makes it a surname rather than a public green space.

title: Park as a surname after Ms.
why: Park is a common surname (notably Korean 박) and an everyday noun. A title and approval predicate select the surname.

ambiguity.note: 'reviewed by' and 'signed by' take agents, and a trade noun without a determiner is not grammatical there.

text: The report was reviewed by Hunter and signed by Mason.
title: Two occupation-word surnames as passive agents
why: 'by Hunter and signed by Mason' places two capitalized words after 'by', the agent position of a passive clause.

ambiguity.note: 'is the title of her first poem' defines the quoted word as a title.

text: "Rose" is the title of her first poem.
title: Quoted work title that is also a given name
why: A word in quotation marks introduced as a title names a poem, not a person.

ambiguity.note: 'Invited X to the opening' selects a person, not a flower.

text: We invited Rose to the opening.
title: Rose as a person invited to an event
why: Rose is a very common flower word; as the object of 'invited' it is a person.

ambiguity.note: 'Did X call' takes an agent subject; the capital letter survives because it is not sentence-initial.

text: Did Rose call before the meeting?
title: Rose as the subject of a polar question
why: A name that is also a flower appears after the auxiliary of a yes/no question, a structure in which a capitalized word cannot be read as sentence-initial.

ambiguity.note: Lowercase 'rose' after the plural subject 'Prices' is the past tense of 'rise'.

title: Lowercase 'rose' as a past-tense verb
why: A lowercase decoy with the exact letters of a common given name. Documents that capitalization is evidence, while the case also guards against a case-insensitive name lookup.

ambiguity.note: Reviewers can recommend a product, an herb or a person.

text: Sage was recommended by several reviewers.
title: Sage as an herb, software or person
why: Sage is an herb, a software product and a given name; a recommendation fits any.

ambiguity.note: 'Song titles' is a noun compound; there is no human referent.

text: Song titles are rarely protected by copyright.
title: Capitalized 'Song' as a noun at sentence start
why: Song is a common surname (including Korean 송). Here it heads a noun compound 'Song titles'.

ambiguity.note: A title precedes it and 'published the results' needs a human agent.

text: Dr. Song published the results last year.
title: Song as a surname after Dr.
why: Partner of song-noun-compound: with a title and an agentive verb, Song is a person.

ambiguity.note: Welcoming someone to a team is an action directed at a person.

text: Please welcome Summer Delaney to the team.
title: Summer as a given name in a full name
why: Summer is a season and a given name. 'Please welcome X to the team' selects a person.

ambiguity.note: 'lists X as virtues' defines the words as abstract nouns.

text: The charter lists Faith, Hope and Charity as virtues.
title: The same virtue nouns in an abstract list
why: Partner of faith-and-hope-as-recipients: here the nouns are abstract terms in a list of values, not recipients.

ambiguity.note: After the title Mr. the word is a surname; the lowercase second is the season.

title: Winter as a surname and as a season
why: A surname and a season with the same spelling in one sentence.

ambiguity.note: 'Young people' is an adjective-noun phrase; the plural noun 'people' follows directly.

text: Young people in the survey mostly agreed.
title: Capitalized 'Young' as an adjective at sentence start
why: Young is a surname; at sentence start it is capitalized by position and here modifies 'people'.

ambiguity.note: After the title 'Mr.', the word can only be a surname.

title: Young as a surname after Mr.
why: Partner of the adjective case: the title makes the same word a surname.

ambiguity.note: Passing salt is something only a person does, which selects the given name.

text: Bill passed the salt across the table.
title: Bill as the agent of a physical handover
why: Partner of bill-legislation-either: a physical, table-side action requires an animate agent, so the same word is a person.

ambiguity.note: In headline or committee-minutes register a bare 'Bill' names a legislative proposal; in running prose it is a given name. Nothing in the sentence marks the register, so both readings stand.

text: Bill passed the committee on Tuesday.
title: Bill as a legislative proposal or a person, transitive passing
why: 'Bill passed the committee' is a standard news-style sentence about legislation and is equally well-formed with a person as the subject; without a determiner the text cannot decide.

ambiguity.note: Approving a budget takes an agent; an award cannot approve, so the active clause selects the person.

text: Grant approved the budget after the second review.
title: Grant as the agent of an approval
why: Partner of grant-passive-either: the same word in subject position of an active verb of approving, which selects an animate agent.

ambiguity.note: In headline or news register a bare 'Grant' names an award that can be approved; in running prose it is a given name whose holder can be approved (for a post or a loan). The text does not mark the register.

text: Grant was approved after the second review.
title: Grant as a funding award or a person, passive clause
why: Sentence-initial capitalization hides whether 'Grant' is a noun or a name, and a passive 'was approved' fits an award and a person. Nothing in the text separates them, so the case records an honest ambiguity.

ambiguity.note: Fading is predicated of feelings and light; a person is not said to fade in this sense.

text: Hope faded as the speech dragged on.
title: Hope as an abstract noun fading
why: Partner of hope-person-arrival: 'faded' is predicated of abstract feelings, so the same capitalized word is a noun and not a mention of a person.

ambiguity.note: Arriving late is predicated of people, and 'the speech had already begun' sets a scene with attendees.

text: Hope arrived late, and the speech had already begun.
title: Hope as a person arriving
why: 'Hope' is an abstract noun and a given name. An arrival predicate selects an animate subject; without it the capitalized sentence-initial word would be a noun.

ambiguity.note: Coordinated with 'Egypt', both are most naturally countries signing a treaty.

text: Jordan and Egypt signed the agreement.
title: Jordan next to another country
why: Coordination with a country name makes the parallel structure political, so 'Jordan' reads as a country.

ambiguity.note: Coordinated with 'Casey', both are most naturally individuals signing for themselves.

text: Jordan and Casey signed the agreement.
title: Jordan next to another given name
why: Partner of jordan-with-country: coordination with a given name makes the parallel structure two people.

ambiguity.note: Metonymy lets a city or institution 'approve' a draft; a person may do so too. No title or first name appears.

title: Lincoln as a person, city or institution, bare subject
why: A bare capitalized surname-or-place as subject of an approval can denote a person or a metonymic institution; the text carries no title, first name or place cue.

ambiguity.note: 'Professor' attaches to people; the surname after it is the person, and the title stays outside the span.

title: Lincoln resolved by a title
why: Partner of lincoln-bare-either: a preceding title selects a person even though the surname is also a place and an institution.

ambiguity.note: Waving is a human gesture; the same name with that predicate denotes a person.

title: Max as a person at the door
why: Partner of max-pet-barking: a human gesture at the same door selects a person.

ambiguity.note: Wagging a tail selects an animal; the span is name-like but not a person in this context.

text: Max wagged his tail at the door.
title: Max as the name of an animal
why: A name-shaped token that names an animal is not a PERSON mention; the tail-wagging predicate selects an animal referent.

ambiguity.note: The idiom 'every Tom, Dick and Harry' is generic and does not denote three individuals.

text: Every Tom, Dick and Harry seems to have an opinion.
title: Tom, Dick and Harry as a fixed expression
why: Three given names in a fixed idiom mean 'anyone at all'. Each token is a name, but the expression refers to no individual; the whole idiom is one not-person span.

ambiguity.note: A sentence-initial modal 'will' would need a subject, so 'Will read' with a bare verb after it is a subject-verb sequence.

text: Will read the testament aloud to the family.
title: Will as the subject of an active reading verb
why: Partner of will-testament-either: an active transitive verb with an inanimate object makes 'Will' the reader. The modal reading is blocked because a modal would need a subject before it.

ambiguity.note: A testament can be announced to a family, and so can a person (for example an arrival or appointment). The text carries no determiner or register cue.

text: Will was announced to the family on Friday.
title: Will as a testament or a person, passive announcement
why: 'Will' is a noun (testament), a modal and a given name; sentence-initial position removes the capitalization cue and 'was announced to the family' fits an announced document and an announced person.

title: Comma-separated record with a name field
why: Comma-separated values without spaces; the name is the first field and the commas are delimiters.

ambiguity.note: The Name,Role header assigns the second cell to the role column.

title: Name and trade role under a header row
why: A header row labels the columns Name and Role, so the second cell of the data row is the role even though it is also a surname.

title: Quoted inverted name in a CSV row
why: A CSV cell in quotes holds a surname-comma-given name; the comma inside the quotes is part of the name, the quotes are not.

projections_excluded.reason: The projection wraps the text in another pair of quotation marks, which would nest with the quotes this case is about and change what it tests.

title: Name inside a JSON-style object
why: Quotes and braces around a name in a key-value structure; the quotes are delimiters and not part of the span.

ambiguity.note: Assignee fields hold people, teams and vendors; the single capitalized value carries no further cue.

title: Assignee label with a value that is also a bank
why: An 'Assignee:' label usually holds a person, but the value 'Chase' is also a financial brand and the field could hold a team or vendor.

ambiguity.note: 'Committee' is a group head noun, so 'Grant' is a modifier of the committee, not a person.

title: Attn label with a committee whose name starts with a given name
why: Partner of label-attn-person: the same label with a committee name that begins with a common given name.

ambiguity.note: The key 'Country' selects a place.

title: Country label with Jordan as the value

title: Lowercase applicant line with a hyphen label
why: A plain-text form line with a hyphen as the separator and all-lowercase content.

ambiguity.note: The key 'Name' selects a personal name.

why: The value Charlotte is also a city; the 'Name:' label says it is a person.

ambiguity.note: The key 'Name' selects a personal name.

title: Name label with Jordan as the value
why: The value Jordan is also a country; the 'Name:' label says it is a person's name.

ambiguity.note: 'Team' is a group head noun; the label alone would not decide.

title: Owner label whose value is a team named after a surname
why: An Owner: label usually takes a person, but a value ending in 'Team' is a group; the head noun decides.

title: Reviewer label with a title and name
why: A label, a title and a name: the title is excluded and the label is not part of the span.

title: Signature label with initials and surname
why: A name written with initials, as on signature lines; the periods are part of the name span.

title: Label-value line with a name
why: Form-style 'Name: value' text with no sentence around the value.

title: Name and role in a semicolon-separated record
why: A record with several fields; only the first field is a person and the second is a job title that looks like a surname-ish word.

ambiguity.note: 'Holdings' is a company head noun; 'v.' separates the parties.

title: Court caption with a person and a company
why: A court caption separates parties with 'v.'; the first is a person, the second a company that reuses a surname.

title: Actor name in a key=value log record
why: A log line has no sentence grammar; the key 'actor=' and the two-token capitalized value are the only cues, and the value ends at the next key.

title: Approver name before a ticket reference
why: A semicolon-delimited record where the approver name is followed by a ticket id with a hyphen and digits.

title: Name after a bracketed severity prefix
why: A bracketed severity tag precedes a normal sentence; the capitalized tag must not be pulled into the name and the name starts after it.

text: level=warn msg="Dana Whitlow failed login twice"
title: Name as the subject of a quoted log message
why: A name inside a quoted msg field of a log line; the quotes delimit the message and are not part of the span.

ambiguity.note: The key 'service' and the head noun 'Gateway' mark a software component.

title: Service name built from a surname
why: A service= field whose value is a surname plus a component noun; the key marks a software component, not a person.

ambiguity.note: A dotted identifier followed by a file:line pair in parentheses is a code reference.

title: Class and method names in a stack frame
why: A stack frame names classes and methods that look like surnames; dotted identifiers inside a frame are code, not people.

ambiguity.note: The key 'thread' says the value identifies a worker, not a person.

title: Thread named like a person
why: A thread= field holding a capitalized common-word name; the key marks a worker thread, not a person.

title: Numbered list of names

title: Reported-by field in a ticket
why: A ticketing-system style field with a label and a full name.

title: Greeting line with a name

ambiguity.note: In a name;place;role row the middle cell is the place.

title: Semicolon-delimited row with a city cell
why: A name;city;role row where the city is a given name too; the semicolons carry no spaces.

title: Sign-off with only a name on the final line
why: A name alone on a line after a closing phrase: the only cue is its position in the message layout.

ambiguity.note: Column position and the full-name cell next to it make the second cell a city.

title: Name beside a city cell
why: A row where the second cell is a city that is also a given name; cells of the same visual shape carry different types.

ambiguity.note: The header 'City' labels the first column, so Savannah is a place and the Owner cell is a person.

title: City column holding a city-like value
why: A header row followed by a data row whose first cell is a city that is also a given name; the header names the column as a city.

title: Name in a pipe-delimited table row
why: A markdown-style row: a name cell, a role cell and a year cell. Pipes sit directly beside the span edges.

title: Tab-separated row
why: Tab-delimited cells have no space around the span; the tab is the only boundary.

ambiguity.note: The 'Ship to:' label introduces an address and 'Lane' is a street head noun.
